title: Swiss inflation persistence and the forecasts a seasonal rule could match
summary: In November 2026 Simon Beyeler returned to a question a Swiss forecaster faced in spring 2022. How much of the recent price increase should enter the estimate of underlying inflation? A related test asks whether that estimate would have produced smaller errors over the next few months. The paper uses an April 2022 information cutoff for the first exercise and repeated forecasts for the second. Their answers matter to different users. A policymaker might want to understand a change in the inflation process, while a forecaster also needs to predict the next published numbers.

The first model divides headline inflation into a persistent component, a short-lived disturbance and a calendar effect. Its estimates of volatility can move over time. This allows the model to put a different weight on a new observation when the historical balance between signal and noise has changed. The seasonal component is especially relevant in Switzerland because the published CPI is unadjusted. A price change that routinely occurs in one month of the year contains less news about the months ahead than the same change at an unusual time.

The second model works with 22 spending categories. Each category can experience persistent and temporary changes of its own and can respond differently to common movements. The estimates put much of the persistence behind the surge in the individual categories. There need not be one dominant common trend for headline inflation to stay elevated. If separate groups continue rising for different reasons, their weighted sum can still rise repeatedly. This distinction also places a limit on the policy interpretation. A statistical component shared across categories is only an estimate of their co-movement. It does not by itself identify demand, supply or monetary policy as the cause.

The study then asks how much hindsight shaped that diagnosis. An estimate produced with data ending in April 2022 already shows the underlying trend moving higher. Its broad agreement with the estimate using later data indicates that the inflation signal was visible at the time. An analyst reading this comparison should keep the date on the estimate. Information available in April could reveal a change in direction without revealing the precise peak later in the year or how quickly the increase would unwind.

Table 1 moves from interpretation to prediction. The target throughout is a three-month change in Swiss CPI. The horizon tells us how far in advance the forecast was produced. Over 180 monthly starting dates, the sectoral model produced an error about 39% smaller than carrying the latest observation forward at the three-month horizon. A seasonal rule that uses the previous year’s corresponding observation did better. Converting the ratios back into percentage points gives approximately 0.535 for the sectoral model and 0.461 for the seasonal rule. Their difference of 0.074 points is an average scoring difference and has no direct interpretation as a forecast bias.

Model selection also depends on the horizon. An autoregression using twelve lags achieved the lowest one-month error in the table. At six months the seasonal rule again scored well, and at twelve months the two simple benchmarks coincide by construction. A forecaster using the paper could retain the category estimates to explain today’s inflation release and publish a separate comparison of forecasting methods at the horizon clients actually use. That decision should also account for the number of independent observations. Adjacent forecast windows overlap, so a run of apparently successful predictions may reflect the same underlying price shock.

questions.question: What does a persistent component mean for the price level that a household pays?
questions.detail: Distinguish a lasting level change from a lasting change in inflation. A one-off increase in a regulated tariff raises the price level indefinitely, even if its contribution to twelve-month inflation disappears a year later. By contrast, a sustained rise in the estimated inflation trend means that prices keep increasing faster over successive periods.

questions.question: What does the paper’s three-month example imply for a forecast competition?
questions.detail: Write down the target and information cutoff before comparing models. For a three-month price change forecast three months ahead, the latest-observation benchmark scores 0.877 points. A model with ratio 0.610 beats that figure, but so does a seasonal rule at 0.526. A ranking against one benchmark alone could therefore lead a forecaster to adopt an unnecessarily complex model.

questions.question: How could a separate test establish whether the apparent seasonal advantage travels?
questions.detail: Freeze each method before evaluating a new block of dates and archive the forecasts as issued. Report paired errors, errors by season and uncertainty allowing for overlap. A stable edge across different inflation environments would support ongoing use. Concentration in a handful of unusual months would instead point to a narrower forecasting advantage.

questions.question: What evidence would support an economic explanation for the sectoral estimates?
questions.detail: Compare the categories showing persistent increases with information on wages, exchange rates, regulated tariffs and producer costs. The timing of those shocks and differences in exposure across categories would help distinguish candidate explanations. The common trend in this model alone cannot do that.

limitation: The estimates are Simon Beyeler’s staff research. They do not represent an official SNB policy forecast. Table 1 tests models against the latest-observation benchmark and supplies no direct significance test between the seasonal rule and the sectoral model.
